title: Your SaaS Product Doesn’t Need More Features. It Might Need a Better Workflow.

It Might Need a Better Workflow. Aakansha Maurya 8 min read · Oct 13, 2026 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Have you ever used a software product that seemed to have everything you needed, yet completing a simple task still felt unnecessarily complicated? You might find yourself switching between dashboards, searching through emails, updating spreadsheets, or following up with different teams just to get one thing done. Interestingly, the problem isn’t always a lack of features. Sometimes, it’s the way those features work together — or fail to. And that’s where an important product management question begins: Are we building more features to solve problems, or are we making it easier for people to get their work done? The problem nobody puts on the feature roadmap Press enter or click to view image in full size Imagine you’re a manager trying to approve a vendor for your company. You open your procurement system to review the request. The vendor’s documents are attached to an email. The finance team has shared its assessment in a spreadsheet. Someone from compliance is waiting for a clarification on another email thread. And the approval itself requires you to log into a different system. The software works. Every tool does what it was designed to do. Yet the task is still difficult. You spend more time finding information, switching between systems, following up with colleagues, and figuring out what happens next than actually making the decision. Now imagine someone proposes a solution: Let’s add a new feature to the procurement dashboard. It sounds reasonable. It’s measurable. It can go into the roadmap. But here’s the question I’d ask before adding it: Will this feature help the manager complete the task, or will it simply give them one more thing to interact with? That distinction matters far more than it might seem. A real-world signal: we’re spending too much time managing work This isn’t just a hypothetical frustration. Microsoft’s 2023 Work Trend Index found that 62% of surveyed workers struggled with spending too much time searching for information during their workday. Its analysis of Microsoft 365 activity also found that employees spent 57% of their time communicating through meetings, email, and chat, compared with 43% creating in applications such as Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. Press enter or click to view image in full size Communication is necessary. Collaboration is necessary. And not every minute spent in a meeting or email is unproductive. But the findings raise a useful product question: how much effort does it take for people to coordinate work before they can actually do it? For enterprise software, that question can be more valuable than asking which feature should be built next. Source: Microsoft Work Trend Index — Will AI Fix Work? Let’s look at the same problem through a product lens Consider a vendor onboarding application. A company wants to onboard a new supplier. The process may involve procurement, finance, legal, and compliance teams. There are two ways a product team could approach the problem. Approach A: Add more features A new dashboard widget. More status filters. Additional reporting options. Another notification setting. The application becomes more capable, but employees may still need to chase documents, re-enter information, and ask other teams for updates. Approach B: Redesign the workflow Collect required information once. Validate documents before submission. Route requests to the right reviewers. Show blockers, ownership, and next steps in one place. Press enter or click to view image in full size The product focuses on helping the user complete the process, not simply giving them more functionality. These are illustrative approaches, not a claim about a particular company’s implementation. In a real product, the right solution would depend on the existing system, user research, technical constraints, and regulatory requirements. Notice the difference: the second approach begins with the job the user needs to complete. That is where product discovery becomes important. The decision product managers need to make When a stakeholder requests a feature, it’s tempting to translate the request directly into a requirement. For example: Stakeholder request: “We need an additional dashboard for vendor approvals.” A product team could immediately start defining the dashboard’s layout, filters, and functionality. But a better discovery conversation would explore a different set of questions: What decision is the stakeholder trying to make? What information do they currently have to collect manually?
